mainTopic: Fixing a מבוי for carrying: the centipede alley, placing the קורה on uneven walls, and using the space under the קורה
overview: This amud finishes one discussion and then opens several new ones about fixing a מבוי so you may carry in it. First, the גמרא explains why רב's ruling about a courtyard breached on two sides is not redundant after the תוספתא. According to רבה, the תוספתא only shows liability for throwing into the courtyard, and רב adds that you may also carry inside it. Next comes a מבוי shaped like a centipede (נדל). אביי's solution is rejected by רבא, who rules according to רב: a צורת הפתח goes on one side of the small alleys, and a לחי or קורה is enough on the other side. Then a chain of teachers named כהנא rules on an alley with one long wall and one short wall. A small difference allows a diagonal קורה. רבא always requires the beam at the end of the short wall, because he holds that a קורה is a היכר and not a מחיצה. רב כהנא adds that a diagonal over ten אמות is invalid according to everyone. The גמרא then asks whether you may use the space under the קורה, brings a dispute of three against three, and shows that the dispute can fit either view of what a קורה is. Finally, רב חסדא and רבא argue about a קורה resting on pegs outside the alley walls. רב אדא בר מתנה begins to challenge רבא from a ברייתא that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the answer: רב adds the case where the breaches are opposite each other
steps.stepSummary: The last line of an answer on the previous amud: the תוספתא covers breaches that do not line up, so רב is needed for breaches that are directly opposite each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the breaches are opposite each other, you might say no, it is not a רשות היחיד. So רב teaches that it still is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it started on the previous amud. It explains what new point רב adds beyond the תוספתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תוספתא only proves that a courtyard breached on two sides is a רשות היחיד when the breaches are not lined up. When they are directly opposite, people might walk straight through, so we might have thought it becomes like a public path. רב's ruling teaches that even then it stays a רשות היחיד.

keyTerms.meaning: one opposite the other: the two breaches line up directly across from each other
I would say no: what we might have wrongly assumed

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the END of an earlier answer, not a new idea. The question it answers (why do we need both רב and the תוספתא?) was asked just before this amud begins.

phrases.english: but if they are one opposite the other,
phrases.notes: Refers to the two breaches in the courtyard wall.

phrases.english: I might say no (it is not a private domain).
phrases.notes: So רב's ruling is needed to teach that it still is.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל זֶה כְּנֶגֶד זֶה, אֵימָא לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer earlier to the question of why רב's ruling is not redundant.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting cases: the תוספתא covers breaches that do not line up, and רב covers breaches that do.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Opposite breaches might turn the courtyard into a walkway and cancel its status as a רשות היחיד.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with opposite breaches, the courtyard stays a רשות היחיד, so רב's ruling is needed.

steps.title: According to רבה, רב's ruling seems to repeat the תוספתא
steps.stepSummary: רבה holds that opposite breaches forbid carrying. So רב must be talking about breaches that do not line up, which is exactly the תוספתא's case. Why do we need both?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבה, who says that when the breaches are opposite each other carrying is forbidden, how does he explain רב's case? It must be where the breaches are not opposite. But then why do I need two rulings saying the same thing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the previous answer by looking at it from רבה's opinion. Under רבה, the answer from step 1 does not work, so רב seems redundant again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 explained רב's ruling as covering opposite breaches. But רבה says opposite breaches make carrying forbidden, so he cannot read רב that way. That forces רבה to place רב's ruling in the case of non-opposite breaches, which the תוספתא already covers. So the question 'why two rulings?' comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: in what case does he set it? (how does he explain the case)
not opposite each other: the breaches do not line up
why do I need two? (a challenge that something is redundant)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up רבה (spelled with a ה at the end) with רבא (spelled with an א at the end). They are two different אמוראים.

phrases.english: And according to Rabba, who said
if they are one opposite the other, it is forbidden,
phrases.notes: Opposite breaches forbid carrying, according to רבה.

phrases.english: this ruling of Rav, in what case does he set it?
in a case where they are not opposite each other,
phrases.notes: The only case left for רב under רבה's view.

phrases.english: why do I need two rulings?
phrases.notes: The תוספתא already covers this case.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבָּה דְּאָמַר זֶה כְּנֶגֶד זֶה אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the answer in step 1 does not fit רבה's opinion, so the question of redundancy comes back.
steps.kashyaTarget: How רבה can explain רב's ruling without it simply repeating the תוספתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under רבה, רב can only be talking about non-opposite breaches. That is the same case as the תוספתא, so one of the two rulings seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The תוספתא is about throwing; רב adds permission to carry
steps.stepSummary: The תוספתא alone would only show liability for throwing into the courtyard. רב teaches that you may also carry inside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If I had only that source (the תוספתא), I would have said its rule applies only to throwing in, but carrying around inside, I would say no. So רב teaches us that carrying is allowed too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that רב and the תוספתא teach two different laws, even though they deal with the same courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תוספתא says the courtyard is a רשות היחיד on the level of Torah law, so someone who throws into it from the public domain is liable. We might still think the חכמים forbade carrying inside it, because so many people pass through it. רב teaches that there is no such decree, and carrying inside is fully permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: if from there: if I had learned only from that other source
I would have said: the mistaken assumption we would have made
these words apply only: limiting a rule to a certain case
to throw: here, throwing from the public domain into the courtyard
to carry or move objects around within the area
he teaches us: introduces the new point (חידוש)

steps.whatToRemember: Even under רבה, רב's ruling is not redundant. The תוספתא tells us there is liability for throwing (Torah-level רשות היחיד). רב tells us carrying inside is permitted (no rabbinic decree).
steps.confusionAlert: Being a רשות היחיד for throwing liability is not automatically the same as being permitted for carrying. The חכמים could have added a decree against carrying even in a place that is a רשות היחיד by Torah law.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern in the גמרא: one source tells us the Torah-level status of a place, and another tells us whether the חכמים added restrictions on top of it.

phrases.english: If from there (the Tosefta) alone, I would have said:
this applies only to throwing,
phrases.notes: There is liability for throwing into it from the public domain.

phrases.english: but to carry within it, I would say no.
phrases.notes: We might have thought the חכמים forbade it because so many people pass through.

phrases.english: He (Rav) teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי מֵהָתָם הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the redundancy challenge from step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separating the topics: the תוספתא is about liability for throwing, and רב is about permission to carry.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The courtyard counts as a רשות היחיד only for throwing liability, while carrying inside would be rabbinically forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Carrying inside the courtyard is permitted. There is no rabbinic decree against it.

steps.title: אביי's ruling on an alleyway shaped like a centipede
steps.stepSummary: A new topic: a main alley with many small side alleys, all open to the public domain. אביי says the big alley needs a צורת הפתח, and the small ones are permitted with a לחי or קורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was said: about an alleyway shaped like a centipede, אביי said that one makes a צורת הפתח for the big alley, and all the small ones are then permitted with a לחי or a קורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a brand-new topic with איתמר, which signals a dispute between אמוראים. Here it brings אביי's view first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The main alley has many small alleys branching off it on both sides, so it is full of openings. אביי requires the stronger fix, a צורת הפתח, for the main alley. The side alleys are treated like regular alleys and only need the simple fix of a לחי or קורה at their openings.

keyTerms.meaning: an alleyway lined with courtyards that opens to the public domain
like a centipede: a main alley with many side alleys branching off it
the form of a doorway: two posts with a beam across the top
a side post placed at the opening of an alley
a beam placed across the top of an alley's opening

steps.confusionAlert: Each side alley here also opens to the public domain on its own. That is why each one needs its own לחי or קורה.

phrases.english: It was stated: an alleyway that is shaped like a centipede,
phrases.notes: A long main alley with small side alleys on both sides.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
one makes a doorway-form for the large alley,
and all those (small alleys) are permitted with a side post or a cross beam.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: מָבוֹי הֶעָשׂוּי כְּנַדָּל, אָמַר אַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Unrelated new topic. The previous discussion has ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a centipede-shaped מבוי, the big alley needs a צורת הפתח, and each small alley needs only a לחי or קורה.

steps.title: רבא asks: אביי's ruling only fits שמואל, and even then the doorway-form is unnecessary
steps.stepSummary: רבא points out that אביי's ruling matches שמואל's view that a bent alley counts as closed. But on that view, why would the big alley need a צורת הפתח?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Whose view are you following? It must be שמואל, who says a bent alley is treated like a closed one. If so, why do you need a צורת הפתח?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the ruling אביי just gave about the big alley with many small side alleys.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי let the small alleys get by with a simple לחי or קורה. That only makes sense if each bend, where a small alley meets the big one, counts as a closed side, which is שמואל's view. But if bends count as closed, the big alley is also just an ordinary alley, and a לחי or קורה should be enough there too.

keyTerms.meaning: According to whom? Which opinion does this follow?
Its law is like a closed alley. This is שמואל's view on a bent alley.
The form of a doorway: two posts with a beam across the top.
A bent, L-shaped alley.

phrases.english: Rava said to him (to Abaye):
According to whom? Like Shmuel,
phrases.notes: Each small alley plus the big alley forms an L-shape, a bent alley.

phrases.english: who said its (a bent alley's) law is like a closed one —
then why does it need a doorway-form?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: כְּמַאן, כִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly challenges אביי's ruling in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's requirement of a צורת הפתח for the big alley
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Inner inconsistency. The leniency for the small alleys assumes שמואל's view. That same view would make the צורת הפתח on the big alley unnecessary.

steps.title: רבא's second challenge: practice in נהרדעא followed רב
steps.stepSummary: Even in נהרדעא, שמואל's own town, people were careful about רב's stricter view on a bent alley. So the הלכה should not be built on שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Furthermore, there was that bent alley in נהרדעא, and they were concerned for רב's view!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a second attack: in practice, the הלכה follows רב, not שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב holds that a bent alley needs a צורת הפתח at the bend. In נהרדעא, where שמואל himself lived, people still followed רב for a real bent alley. So a ruling that relies on שמואל's view cannot be correct in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore. Introduces an added challenge.
נהרדעא, the town where שמואל lived.
They were concerned for it (took that view into account).

phrases.english: And furthermore, there was that bent alley
that was in Nehardea,
and they were concerned for the view of Rav!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹד, הָא הָהוּא מָבוֹי עָקוֹם דַּהֲוָה בִּנְהַרְדְּעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, practical challenge to the theoretical one in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: Basing the ruling on שמואל's view at all
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Proof from practice. Even in שמואל's own town, they followed רב on bent alleys.

steps.title: רבא's own solution for the centipede alley
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that you make a צורת הפתח for all the small alleys on one side, and the other side is permitted with a לחי or קורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: You make a צורת הפתח for all of them on this side. The other side becomes permitted with a לחי or a קורה.
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected אביי's approach, רבא gives his own ruling, which follows רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב requires a צורת הפתח at the bend of a bent alley. So each small alley gets a צורת הפתח where it bends into the big alley. The other end of each small alley, which opens straight to the public domain, only needs the regular לחי or קורה.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. Replaces a rejected approach with a new one.
Side.
A side post placed at the entrance of an alley.
A crossbeam placed across the entrance of an alley.

steps.whatToRemember: On the centipede alley, the final ruling is רבא's, which follows רב. Put a צורת הפתח on the side where the small alleys bend into the big one. Use a לחי or קורה on the other side.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
One makes a doorway-form
for all of them on this side,
and the other side
is permitted with a side post or crossbeam.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: עוֹשֶׂה צוּרַת הַפֶּתַח לְכוּלְּהוּ לְהַאי גִּיסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's ruling after the two challenges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A צורת הפתח goes on the bend side of all the small alleys. A לחי or קורה is enough on the other side.

steps.title: Alley with one long wall and one short wall
steps.stepSummary: A chain of teachers in the name of רב כהנא, רב's teacher, gives the rule. If the walls differ by less than four אמות, the קורה goes diagonally. If they differ by four אמות or more, it goes straight across at the end of the short wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא בר תחליפא said in the name of a chain of teachers, ending with רב כהנא, the teacher of רב. (Some say רב כהנא בר מלכיו is the same person as רב כהנא, the teacher of רב.) The rule: In an alley where one wall is long and the other is short, if the difference is less than four אמות, the קורה is placed diagonally. If it is four אמות, the קורה is placed only straight across at the end of the short wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a brand-new case about an alley whose two side walls stick out unevenly into the public domain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is where the קורה goes when one wall sticks out further than the other. For a small difference (under four אמות), the beam can stretch diagonally from the end of one wall to the end of the other. For a big difference, the beam must go straight across at the end of the short wall, and the extra part beyond it cannot be used.

keyTerms.meaning: In the name of.
Diagonally.
Opposite (at the end of) the short wall.
Four אמות (cubits).

steps.confusionAlert: The four רב כהנא's are a chain of transmission, one quoting the next. It is not four separate opinions. The 'some say' line only asks whether two of the names are the same person.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana bar Tachlifa said
in the name of Rav Kahana bar Minyumi,
in the name of Rav Kahana bar Malkiyu,
in the name of Rav Kahana, the teacher of Rav;

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לָהּ, רַב כָּהֲנָא בַּר מַלְכִּיּוֹ
phrases.english: and some say: Rav Kahana bar Malkiyu
is the same as Rav Kahana, the teacher of Rav:
An alley whose one side is long
and whose other side is short,
if the difference is less than four cubits,
one places the crossbeam diagonally.
If it is four cubits —
one does not place the crossbeam
except opposite the short side.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא בַּר תַּחְלִיפָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic, still about the rules for setting up a קורה or לחי on an alley.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under four אמות difference, the קורה goes diagonally. At four אמות or more, it goes at the end of the short wall.

steps.title: רבא disagrees: always at the end of the short wall
steps.stepSummary: רבא holds that in both cases, small difference or big, the קורה goes only at the end of the short wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: In both this case and that case, the קורה is placed only straight across at the end of the short wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא disagrees with רב כהנא and rejects the diagonal option completely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא allowed a diagonal beam when the difference was small. רבא gives no such leniency: the beam must always go straight across at the end of the short wall, even for a tiny difference.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this and that. Same rule in both cases.

phrases.english: Rava said:
In both this case and that case,
one does not place the crossbeam
except opposite the short side.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a disagreeing view on the case from step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The קורה is never placed diagonally. It always goes at the end of the short wall.

steps.title: רבא sets up his reasoning: what is the purpose of a crossbeam?
steps.stepSummary: רבא announces he will explain his own reason and theirs. He starts by asking what job the קורה does.
steps.simpleTranslation: I will say my reason, and I will say their reason. My reason: What is the reason for a קורה?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. רבא is preparing to justify his view by first asking what a קורה is for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To decide where the beam may go, you first need to know what it is supposed to accomplish. רבא lays out that question here so his answer in the next step can rule out the diagonal.

keyTerms.meaning: My reason.
Their reason.
What is the reason?

phrases.english: And I will say my reason,
and I will say their reason.
I will say my reason:
a crossbeam, what is its reason? —

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא טַעְמָא דִידִי, וְאֵימָא טַעְמָא דִידְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the explanation of רבא's ruling from step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the function of a קורה?

steps.title: A crossbeam is a visible marker, and a diagonal one is not visible enough
steps.stepSummary: A קורה works as a היכר, a visible sign of the alley's boundary. A diagonal beam does not make a clear enough sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of a visible marker, and on a diagonal it is not a visible marker.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers his own question: the קורה is a marker, and a diagonal beam fails as a marker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קורה shows people where the permitted alley ends and the public domain begins. A slanted beam leaves part of the area beyond the short wall looking like it is inside. People might see carrying there and think carrying in a public domain is allowed. So the beam must go straight across at the end of the short wall.

keyTerms.meaning: A visible marker or sign.
It is not.

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main dispute. Does the קורה work as a היכר (רבא's view) or for another reason (רב כהנא's view, which רבא is about to explain)? The answer decides where it may be placed.

phrases.english: because of a visible marker,
and on a diagonal it is not a marker.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם הֶיכֵּר, וּבַאֲלַכְסוֹן לָא הָוֵי הֶיכֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question posed in step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A קורה serves as a היכר, and a diagonal placement does not make a clear היכר.

steps.title: The other side's reason: a beam counts as a wall
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the view of רב כהנא's teachers. They hold that a קורה works as a מחיצה, and a wall still works even when it is diagonal.
steps.simpleTranslation: And I will also explain their reason: why does a קורה work? Because it counts as a מחיצה (a wall). And a diagonal wall is still a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes the explanation he promised in Step 10. He already gave his own reason, and now he gives the reason of the teachers who allow a diagonal קורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 11, רבא said a קורה is a היכר, a sign, and a diagonal sign is not clear enough. The other side says a קורה acts like a wall that closes the alley. A wall does its job even if it runs at a slant, so a diagonal קורה is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: Their reason (the reason of the other opinion)
A partition or wall; here, the idea that the beam counts as a fourth wall
Diagonal, at a slant

steps.whatToRemember: The whole argument about the diagonal קורה comes down to one question. Is a קורה a היכר (sign), so it must be straight and clear? Or is it a מחיצה (wall), so a diagonal is fine?
steps.whyThisMatters: This היכר-or-מחיצה split comes up again in Step 16 to explain a completely different argument.

phrases.english: And I will say their reason:
A cross beam works because of what?
Because it counts as a partition (wall).
And even diagonally, it is a partition.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא טַעְמָא דִידְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's two-part explanation. Step 11 gave his own reason, and this step gives the opposing reason.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The other opinion holds that a קורה works as a מחיצה, and a wall still works when it is diagonal.

steps.title: רב כהנא limits the diagonal beam to ten אמות
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא says the diagonal קורה is allowed only if the diagonal is ten אמות or less. If the diagonal is more than ten, everyone agrees the beam goes straight across at the short wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: since this teaching comes from people named כהנא, let me add something. What you said, that the קורה can be placed diagonally, applies only when the diagonal is not more than ten אמות. But if the diagonal is more than ten אמות, everyone agrees the beam must be placed straight across, at the end of the short wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא adds a limit to the rule from Step 8 about placing the קורה diagonally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קורה can only fix an alley entrance that is ten אמות wide or less. A diagonal line is longer than the straight width of the alley. So even if the alley itself is narrower than ten, the diagonal may be longer than ten. In that case even the teachers who allow a diagonal agree it cannot be used, and the beam goes straight across at the short wall.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching of people named כהנא (a light play on his own name)
More than ten (אמות), the widest entrance a קורה can fix
Everyone agrees
Opposite (at the end of) the short wall

steps.confusionAlert: The ten-אמה limit is measured along the slanted beam itself, not across the straight width of the alley. An alley that is less than ten wide can still have a diagonal longer than ten.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
Since this is a teaching of the Kahanas,
I will say something about it.
That which you said,
that one places the cross beam diagonally,
we only said this
where its diagonal is not more than ten (cubits),
but if its diagonal is more than ten,
all agree
he places it only straight across, at the short side.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוֹאִיל וּשְׁמַעְתְּתָא דְכָהֲנֵי הִיא, אֵימָא בַּהּ מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the diagonal-beam ruling that Steps 8 and 12 defended, by adding the ten-אמה limit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A diagonal קורה works only if the diagonal is ten אמות or less. Beyond that, everyone requires the beam to go straight across at the short wall.

steps.title: New question: may one carry under the beam?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new question: is it allowed to use the space directly beneath the קורה?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: what is the law about using (carrying in) the space under the קורה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. The קורה makes the alley a permitted place to carry, but is the strip right under the beam part of that permitted area? The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion was about where to put the beam. Now the question is whether the area under the beam counts as inside the alley or not. This is a new line of discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them (an open question of the Sages)
To use; here, to carry in that space on שבת
Beneath the cross beam

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
What is the law about using the area beneath the cross beam?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the placement discussion and opens a new question about the status of the area under the beam.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether it is allowed to carry in the space directly beneath the קורה.

steps.title: Three permit and three forbid using the space under the beam
steps.stepSummary: רב, רבי חייא, and רבי יוחנן permit using the space under the קורה. שמואל, רבי שמעון בר רבי, and רבי שמעון בן לקיש forbid it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב, רבי חייא, and רבי יוחנן said: it is permitted to use the space under the קורה. שמואל, רבי שמעון בר רבי, and רבי שמעון בן לקיש said: it is forbidden to use the space under the קורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a dispute. Two groups of three Sages each take opposite positions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question does not get one answer. It is a real argument: one group treats the area under the beam as part of the permitted alley, and the other group does not. Notice the pairing. Each permitting Sage is matched by a well-known partner who forbids it (רב and שמואל, רבי חייא and רבי שמעון בר רבי, רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש).

keyTerms.meaning: Permitted
Forbidden

phrases.aramaic: רַב וְרַבִּי חִיָּיא וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמְרוּ:
phrases.english: Rav, Rabbi Ḥiyya, and Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
It is permitted to use the area beneath the cross beam.
Shmuel and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said:
It is forbidden to use the area beneath the cross beam.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב וְרַבִּי חִיָּיא וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 14 with a two-sided dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dispute: רב, רבי חייא, and רבי יוחנן permit using the space under the קורה. שמואל, רבי שמעון בר רבי, and ריש לקיש forbid it.

steps.title: Suggestion: the argument depends on sign versus wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the dispute about the space under the קורה comes from the same split seen before. Those who permit hold that a קורה is a היכר, and those who forbid hold that a קורה is a מחיצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they argue about this? One Sage holds that a קורה works as a היכר (sign), and the other Sage holds that a קורה works as a מחיצה (wall).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to find the root of the dispute from Step 15. It connects it to the היכר-or-מחיצה question from Steps 11 and 12. The word לימא means this is only a proposal, which the גמרא will now test.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the proposal, the Sages who permit hold the beam is just a sign of the boundary, so the space under it counts as inside the alley. The Sages who forbid hold the beam is a wall. On that view, the space under it is part of the wall line and does not count as inside the permitted area. Since this starts with לימא, the גמרא may still reject this explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (introduces a suggestion that may be rejected)
They argue (about this point)
One master holds

steps.confusionAlert: לימא does not give a final answer. It is a trial suggestion, and the גמרא often goes on to reject it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the two views, היכר and מחיצה, are not limited to the diagonal question. They may explain other laws of the קורה too.

phrases.english: Shall we say they argue about this:
that one master holds: a cross beam works as a conspicuous marker,
and the other master holds: a cross beam works as a partition.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא בְּהָא קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a conceptual root for the dispute of Step 15, using the היכר-or-מחיצה split from Steps 11 and 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the dispute about using the space under the קורה depends on whether a קורה is a היכר or a מחיצה.

steps.title: Everyone may agree the beam is a marker, and the argument is about who the marker is for
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the link from step 16. Everyone may hold קורה משום היכר. They argue only about whether the marker is meant for people inside the alley or for people outside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone may agree that a beam works as a marker. Here they argue about this: one master holds the marker is for people inside, and the other master holds the marker is for people outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says 'No' to the idea that the dispute about the space under the קורה matches the היכר-versus-מחיצה dispute. It shows that both sides can agree the קורה is a היכר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the marker is aimed at the people inside, the alley ends at the beam's inner edge, so the space under it is forbidden. If the marker is aimed at the people outside in the רשות הרבים, the alley stretches to the beam's outer edge, so the space under it is permitted. The disagreement is about where the marker 'faces', not about what a קורה is.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
A noticeable marker or reminder
They disagree
From the inside (for those inside)
From the outside (for those outside)

steps.confusionAlert: Match the sides carefully. 'Marker for the inside' belongs to the side that forbids using the space under the beam. 'Marker for the outside' belongs to the side that permits it.

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees
phrases.notes: Rejects the suggestion from step 16

phrases.english: that a beam works as a marker,
and here they argue about this:
one master holds the marker is for those inside,
phrases.notes: This is the side that forbids. The alley ends at the inner edge.

phrases.english: and the other master holds the marker is for those outside.
phrases.notes: This is the side that permits. The alley reaches the outer edge.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא קוֹרָה מִשּׁוּם הֶיכֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 16's claim that the dispute depends on היכר versus מחיצה
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects tying the dispute about the space under the beam to the dispute about the nature of the קורה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Both sides can hold that a קורה is a היכר and still disagree, about whom the marker is aimed at

steps.title: Everyone may agree the beam is a partition, and the argument is about which edge counts
steps.stepSummary: A second way to reject the link. Everyone may hold קורה משום מחיצה. They argue only about whether the inner edge or the outer edge of the beam 'comes down' to form the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say that everyone agrees the beam works as a partition. Here they argue about this: one master holds that the beam's inner edge comes down and closes off the alley, and the other master holds that its outer edge comes down and closes it off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to reject the link. This time both sides agree the קורה is a מחיצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We imagine the edge of the beam dropping down to the ground like a wall (חוד יורד וסותם). If the inner edge is the wall, the space under the beam is outside the alley and forbidden. If the outer edge is the wall, the space under the beam is inside the alley and permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (introduces another answer)
A partition or wall
Its inner edge
Its outer edge
Comes down and closes off (an imagined wall)

steps.whatToRemember: The dispute about the space under the קורה does not have to depend on the היכר-versus-מחיצה dispute. It works with either view.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
everyone agrees it works as a partition,
and here they argue about this:
one master holds that its inner edge
comes down and closes off the alley,
phrases.notes: So the space under the beam is forbidden

phrases.english: and the other master holds that its outer edge
comes down and closes off the alley.
phrases.notes: So the space under the beam is permitted

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מִשּׁוּם מְחִיצָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, alternative rejection of step 16, this time from the מחיצה side
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the same link from step 16 again
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Both sides can hold that a קורה is a מחיצה and still disagree, about which edge forms the imagined wall

steps.title: Everyone agrees the space between the side posts is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that everyone, even those who permit the space under the קורה, agrees that the space between the לחיים may not be used.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Everyone agrees that the space between the side posts is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא adds a ruling that all the opinions agree on. Using the area between the two לחיים at the alley entrance is not allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A לחי works as a מחיצה, so the alley ends at its inner edge. The space between the לחיים is therefore outside the permitted area. The argument about the קורה does not reach this case.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
Side posts at the entrance of an alley
Forbidden

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets a clear limit. Whatever the dispute about the קורה, the area between the לחיים is not part of the permitted alley.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
everyone agrees about the space between the side posts
that it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: הַכֹּל מוֹדִים בְּבֵין לְחָיַיִם שֶׁאָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the dispute from step 15: it does not apply to the space between the לחיים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using the space between the לחיים is forbidden according to everyone

steps.title: What if the beam rests on pegs on the outside of the alley walls?
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks רב חסדא about a קורה placed on two pegs that stick out from the outer side of the alley walls, instead of on top of the walls. Does it work?
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא asked רב חסדא: If someone stuck two pegs into the two walls of the alley on the outside, and put a beam on top of them, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question opens. רמי בר חמא asks whether a קורה still works when it rests on pegs attached to the outside face of the alley walls instead of sitting on the walls themselves. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the קורה sits on top of the alley walls. Here it hangs in front of the entrance, attached from the outside. The question is whether a beam in this position still permits carrying in the מבוי.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him
Pegs
The walls of the alley
On the outside
What is the law?

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא מֵרַב חִסְדָּא:
phrases.english: Rami bar Chama asked Rav Chisda:
if someone stuck two pegs
into the two walls of the alley, on the outside,
and placed a beam on top of them,
what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא מֵרַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about where the קורה is placed
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a קורה resting on pegs on the outside of the alley walls permits carrying in the מבוי

steps.title: רב חסדא answers: the two opinions flip for a beam on outside pegs
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא answers רמי בר חמא. According to the one who permits the space under the קורה, this setup is forbidden. According to the one who forbids that space, it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said to him: According to the one who permits using the space under the beam, it is forbidden. According to the one who forbids, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the question from step 20 about a קורה resting on pegs just outside the alley. He says the answer depends on the two opinions explained in step 18.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one who permits the space under the קורה holds that the outer edge 'comes down' to form a wall. Here the outer edge sits fully outside the alley, so it cannot close the alley, and carrying is forbidden. The one who forbids that space holds that the inner edge 'comes down'. Here the inner edge touches the alley's entrance, so it closes the alley, and carrying is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who permits (using the space under the קורה)
The one who forbids (using the space under the קורה)
Forbidden / permitted (to carry in the alley)

steps.confusionAlert: This looks backwards at first. The lenient opinion about the space under the beam becomes strict here, and the strict opinion becomes lenient. It flips because each opinion depends on WHICH edge of the beam counts as the wall, not on being lenient or strict in general.

phrases.english: He said to him: According to the one who permits, it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: The permitter holds the outer edge forms the wall. Here that edge is fully outside the alley.

phrases.english: According to the one who forbids, it is permitted.
phrases.notes: The forbidder holds the inner edge forms the wall. Here that edge touches the alley's entrance.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְדִבְרֵי הַמַּתִּיר — אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question רמי בר חמא asked in step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The beam on outside pegs is forbidden according to the one who permits the space under the קורה, and permitted according to the one who forbids it. This follows from which edge of the beam 'comes down'.

steps.title: רבא disagrees: the beam must sit on top of the alley walls
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects רב חסדא's leniency for the forbidder. Even the one who forbids the space under the קורה forbids this setup, because a קורה must rest on top of the alley, and here it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Even according to the one who forbids, it is forbidden. We need the beam to be on top of the alley, and it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא disagrees with half of רב חסדא's answer. He says the setup is forbidden according to both opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא only looked at which edge 'comes down'. רבא adds a basic requirement that comes first: the קורה must actually lie on top of the alley's walls. A beam that only touches the alley from the outside fails that requirement, so the question of edges never comes up.

keyTerms.meaning: Also / even
We require
On top of the alley (resting on its walls)
And it is not there (the requirement is missing)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a rule that comes before the edge debate: the beam must physically rest on the alley. רב אדא בר מתנה will now test this rule against a ברייתא.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא אָמַר: לְדִבְרֵי הָאוֹסֵר נָמֵי אָסוּר —
phrases.english: Rava said: Even according to the one who forbids, it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: רבא disagrees with רב חסדא's 'permitted' for the forbidder.

phrases.aramaic: בָּעִינַן קוֹרָה עַל גַּבֵּי מָבוֹי, וְלֵיכָּא.
phrases.english: We require a beam on top of the alley, and there is none.
phrases.notes: The beam is only next to the alley from outside, not resting on its walls.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: לְדִבְרֵי הָאוֹסֵר נָמֵי אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the second half of רב חסדא's answer in step 21.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only רב חסדא's ruling that the forbidder permits. רבא agrees the permitter forbids.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב חסדא missed a basic requirement: the קורה must rest on top of the alley walls, not hang just outside them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A קורה must lie on top of the alley. A beam on pegs outside the alley is invalid according to everyone.

steps.title: רב אדא בר מתנה begins to challenge רבא from a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר מתנה raises an objection to רבא and starts quoting a ברייתא that begins 'If its beam was...'. The quote continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר מתנה raised an objection to רבא: 'If its beam was...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge to רבא. רב אדא בר מתנה starts quoting a ברייתא about where an alley's beam is placed, and the rest of the quote comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אֵיתִיבֵיהּ tells us a source is being brought to attack a view. Here the target is רבא's rule that a קורה must be on top of the alley. We must wait for the rest of the ברייתא to see the exact problem.

keyTerms.meaning: If its beam was... (the opening words of the ברייתא)

phrases.aramaic: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָה לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Mattana raised an objection to Rava:
phrases.notes: This introduces a challenge from a ברייתא.

phrases.english: If its beam was...
phrases.notes: The ברייתא continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָה לְרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's rule from step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that a קורה must rest on top of the alley walls.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא about where an alley's beam may be placed seems to conflict with רבא's requirement. The full wording appears on the next amud.
